newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat-U.S. talks on power plants in final stage.
newsitem.headline: Croat-U.S. talks on power plants in final stage.

text.p: ZAGREB, July 24 - Croatian utility HEP said on Friday it had nearly reached agreement with U.S. Enron Corp and Enserch International Inc to develop power plants valued at $1.0 billion.
"Our negotiations on Independent Power Producer (IPP) programmes have entered the final stage," HEP's production director Ante Curkovic told Reuters.
Last July the U.S. companies signed a letter of understanding with HEP, which gave them 18 months to present a detailed proposal on building three coal and gas-fired plants.
HEP had reserved its right to consider offers by other interested parties.

Last year HEP president Damir Begovic said Enserch would prepare one or two $500 million projects for 350 MW coal-fired plants and said Enron had expressed interest in building and operating a gas-fired combined cycle plant.
"One of the key elements for Enron was to provide gas, while competitive prices were the most important factor for the Enserch proposal," Curkovic said.

The introduction of foreign suppliers and owners into the energy sector would signal a new direction in Croatian government policy. Until now HEP has had a monopoly over power production and distribution in the former Yugoslav republic.
"We are about to take an international test and prove our ability to negotiate," said Curkovic.
HEP expects to sign the agreement with Enron in three to four months' time and Enserch should follow soon after that.

"We are glad to enjoy support by the Croatian government," Enron's deputy president Joseph Sutton, who visited Croatia, told state television late on Thursday, particularly because this venture "is the first American investment in Croatia's infrastructure".
If the contract is signed Enron will begin building the 150-180 MW plant 30 km from Zagreb next year, the television report said.

"This particular investment is of the greatest significance for our energy sector," Begovic told the television. "It will considerably improve the power supply in the city of Zagreb as Croatia's biggest consumption centre," he added.
HEP said first deliveries were expected late in 1999.
